title: HIS-201 Ch. 3 — 4 Main Ideas
subject: HIS-201
topic: Chapter 3: Colonization and Conflict in the South

cards.term: Why Powhatan tolerated the English
cards.def: Powhatan considered the colonists a nuisance but let them survive because English trade goods and weapons helped him strengthen his rule and fend off Piedmont tribes.

cards.term: How Spain colonized the Southwest and Florida
cards.def: Spain held its northern borderlands with scattered military garrisons, cattle ranches, and missions staffed by Dominican and Franciscan priests.

cards.term: Why Spain's northern colonies stayed small
cards.def: New Mexico and Florida were poor and dangerous, so few Spaniards settled there, and the colonies survived mainly as missions and military buffers.

cards.term: The lesson of Acoma
cards.def: The Acoma massacre taught the Pueblos that resistance brought terror, but Spanish brutality also destroyed the cooperation New Mexico needed to prosper.

cards.term: Why Spain kept New Mexico
cards.def: The Franciscans persuaded the Crown to keep unprofitable New Mexico by arguing that abandoning baptized Indians would betray Catholic duty.

cards.term: The causes of the Pueblo Revolt
cards.def: Forced labor, disease, famine, Apache raids, and Spanish repression of Pueblo religion united the Pueblos to rise against Spanish rule.

cards.term: How mercantilism drove colonization
cards.def: Mercantilism encouraged European monarchs to sponsor colonies because colonies supplied raw materials, bought finished goods, and increased royal revenue and power.

cards.term: The significance of the Virginia Company
cards.def: The Virginia Company planted England's first permanent colony, and its land and political reforms laid the foundation for Virginia's growth before its failures led to royal rule.

cards.term: Why Jamestown nearly failed
cards.def: Jamestown nearly collapsed because gentlemen refused to work, settlers lacked farming skills, disease and brackish water spread, and colonists demanded food from Indians.

cards.term: How Virginia's reforms attracted settlers
cards.def: The headright system, an elected assembly, and relaxed martial law attracted migrants and investment, allowing Virginia's tobacco economy to expand.

cards.term: The significance of the headright system
cards.def: The headright system rewarded planters who imported laborers with more land, so it drove the flood of indentured servants and the growth of large tobacco plantations.

cards.term: The consequences of the tobacco boom
cards.def: Tobacco profits drove relentless seizure of Indian land and constant demand for labor, causing Indian wars and dependence on indentured servants before slavery prevailed.

cards.term: The cycle of Indian wars in the Chesapeake
cards.def: The Chesapeake Indians, organized in an effective confederacy, went to war whenever a new generation of men came of age, in 1622, 1644, and 1675.

cards.term: How Maryland differed from Virginia
cards.def: Maryland combined family proprietary rule, Catholic leadership, and toleration for all Christians, making it both a Catholic refuge and Virginia's tobacco rival.

cards.term: How England took greater control of its colonies
cards.def: England tightened control by making Virginia, South Carolina, and Georgia royal colonies, passing the Navigation Acts, and adopting Charles II's consistent colonial policy.

cards.term: The causes of Bacon's Rebellion
cards.def: Falling tobacco prices, landless freed servants, Indian conflict, and exclusion from power united frontier farmers and ambitious gentlemen against Berkeley's government.

cards.term: How the Navigation Acts affected the Chesapeake
cards.def: The Navigation Acts strengthened England's mercantilist empire but restricted Chesapeake trade and deepened planters' distress as tobacco prices fell.

cards.term: How slavery evolved in the early South
cards.def: In the early Chesapeake some blacks were free or indentured and had more rights, but harsh slave codes followed once larger numbers arrived directly from West Africa.

cards.term: How slavery united white society
cards.def: As slavery replaced servitude, fear of the growing black population drew whites of all classes and religions into a racist consensus led by a new gentry.

cards.term: How the slave trade transformed West Africa
cards.def: Slave trading enriched African rulers who built stronger states, while warfare, kidnapping, famine, and disease drew interior communities into bondage.

cards.term: The scale of Atlantic slavery
cards.def: The Atlantic slave trade carried far more Africans than Europeans to the Americas, making African workers central to every plantation economy.

cards.term: The characteristics of the Caribbean sugar economy
cards.def: Sugar turned the English Caribbean into deadly, black-majority slave societies of great wealth, and Britain valued the West Indies as its most valuable American possession.

cards.term: How Caribbean planters controlled enslaved people
cards.def: Caribbean blacks never had a period of rough frontier equality, because sugar planters enacted brutal slave laws early to control the slaves who soon dominated the islands.

cards.term: The economic origins of South Carolina
cards.def: Land scarcity on Barbados sent planters to found South Carolina, which grew rich exporting rice and later indigo with the skilled labor of a black majority.

cards.term: How African expertise built South Carolina's rice economy
cards.def: South Carolina's rice wealth depended on enslaved Africans' knowledge of rice growing, yet white fear of the black majority produced Caribbean-style slave codes.

cards.term: How Carolina's Indian slave trade reshaped the Southeast
cards.def: Carolina traders turned Indian slavery into a major business, devastating Florida's missions and neighboring peoples until the Yamasee War ended the trade.

cards.term: The result of the Yamasee War
cards.def: The Yamasee War nearly destroyed South Carolina and ended proprietary rule, and the colony won only with Cherokee help, while southeastern confederacies learned to balance rival empires.

cards.term: The trustees' plan for Georgia
cards.def: Georgia's trustees banned slavery and liquor and limited landholding so the colony could be a buffer against Spanish Florida and a refuge of small farms.

cards.term: How North Carolina, South Carolina, and Georgia differed
cards.def: South Carolina grew rich on rice and slaves, North Carolina stayed a poor colony of small farms and naval stores, and Georgia began as a slave-free buffer and refuge.

cards.term: How North Carolina, South Carolina, and Georgia were alike
cards.def: All three colonies began under proprietors or trustees, ended as royal colonies, and ultimately depended on plantation agriculture and enslaved labor.

cards.term: How Europeans changed Native American societies in the South
cards.def: Europeans spread disease, forced Indians into missions, seized land for tobacco, and drew them into the slave trade, wrecking older ways of life across the South.

cards.term: The common pattern of southern colonies
cards.def: Southern colonies shared staple-crop economies, close ties to English merchants, inequality among whites, racial slavery, and Indian dispossession.

cards.term: The staple crops of the southern colonies
cards.def: The Chesapeake specialized in tobacco, South Carolina in rice and indigo, and the Caribbean in sugar, tying each region's wealth to coerced labor.

cards.term: Why Indian-settler relations differed across the southern colonies
cards.def: Disease and slavery had nearly erased Caribbean Indians before English settlement, Chesapeake peoples fought back through a strong confederacy, and South Carolina drew many Indians into trading pelts and captives.
